data_quirks.description: -1 is the missing-value sentinel in every column, categorical and numeric alike: 'Values of -1 indicate that the feature was missing from the observation.' The columns with substantial missingness are ps_car_03_cat, ps_car_05_cat, ps_reg_03 and ps_car_14. For a spline model the sentinel MUST be routed out of the numeric range (own level / separate band), or the smooth will be dragged by a spike at -1.

The 1st place deliberately did no imputation at all - '-1' was fed to the models as a live value and it still won: 'No missing value replacement or something.' The 2nd place instead added a row-level count of -1s. Both treatments are documented winners; imputation to a mean is documented by nobody.

Column names encode the variable group and the type: the prefixes ind / reg / car / calc mark 'similar groupings', the postfix _bin marks a binary feature and _cat marks a categorical; everything else is continuous or ordinal. Two teams exploited the group structure directly (the 2nd place's cross-group XGBoost predictions, the 12th place's per-block NN weight matrices).

Severe class imbalance: roughly 3.6-4% of rows have target = 1 ('only approximately 4% of policyholders filing claims'). CPMP set xgboost scale_pos_weight = 3 and min_child_weight = 6 with the explicit rationale of going only as deep as isolates at least two claims - the practical warning is that per-cell claim counts are tiny, so tensor cells must be coarse or strongly penalised.

No exposure, term or date column exists in the table - each row is one policy over a one-year horizon, so there is no offset to fit and no time split to respect. Jahrer: 'leakage-free, time-free and statistical correct dataset'.

Fold-to-fold Gini variance is very large; both CPMP and the 2nd place team say the public LB was unreliable and that seed-averaging (CPMP: 5 CV repeats x 5 folds x 3 seeds = 75 models; 2nd place: averaging across seeds) was what stabilised the score. Any A/B comparison of feature sets on this data needs repeated CV, not one fold.

ps_car_11_cat is a high-cardinality categorical (104 levels) and is the natural target for level-count / frequency encoding rather than plain one-hot; ps_ind_05_cat is the one categorical the 2nd place team used as a grouping key for numeric aggregates.

The test set (892,816 rows) is larger than the training set (595,212 rows); the 1st place used train+test jointly for unsupervised learning, and the 2nd place computed all count/aggregate features on train+test concatenated. If count features are used in an offline replication, compute them on the same population the winners did or the values will not match.

data_quirks.description: The data is fully anonymised: Kaggle's description says only 'Each row in this dataset represents an insurance claim. You must predict the value for the loss column. Variables prefaced with cat are categorical, while those prefaced with cont are continuous.' There is no column dictionary, no date, no exposure and no weight column. The 2nd place winner states he tried and failed to reverse-engineer meaning: 'I tried to find some meaningful features, but had no success at it.'

Metric is MAE, confirmed from the archived competition page: evaluationAlgorithm {id: 6, name: 'Mean Absolute Error'} and 'Submissions are evaluated on the mean absolute error (MAE) between the predicted loss and the actual loss.' MAE targets the conditional median, so a mean-fitted model is systematically mis-aimed; the 2nd place solution finished with a median (quantile) regression at level 3 and with an explicit power-bias correction of its mean-fitted stack.

loss is strongly right-skewed and its minimum is well below 1 (values such as 0.67 exist), so log(loss) produces negative values -- that is the stated reason the winners used a shifted log, log(loss + 200).

cont14 is not a plain continuous variable: the 2nd place de-skewing code treats it as supported on [0.179722, 0.844844] via (max(cont14 - 0.179722, 0) / 0.665122) ** 0.25, i.e. it has a hard lower bound at 0.179722 and a range of 0.665122, with a clip for anything below the bound. It is also the one variable he commented out of his hand-built feature block. Check for a point mass at the lower bound before smoothing it.

The continuous columns are strongly mutually correlated in two clusters -- {cont1, cont6, cont9, cont10} and {cont6, cont7, cont11, cont12, cont13} -- which is why the 2nd place pipeline carries eleven pairwise differences rather than the raw levels. An independent analysis confirms 'there are some strong relationship between some variables'. data_quirks.description: NO DOCUMENTED PAIRWISE INTERACTION EXISTS FOR THIS COMPETITION. This is the headline finding. The 1st-place winner says outright: 'Since the variables were anonymous there wasn't much feature engineering to be done. Instead I treated feature engineering as just another parameter to tune' and 'I also played with different encodings of categorical variables and interactions, nothing sophisticated'. The metric is rank-only: 'To calculate the normalized Gini, your predictions are sorted from largest to smallest. This is the only step where the explicit prediction values are used (i.e. only the order of your predictions matters).' Consequences for a GAM arm: (a) any monotone transform of the fitted values is score-neutral, so a log link costs nothing; (b) calibration is irrelevant and only the induced ordering matters; (c) the metric is insensitive to the scale parameter, so REML/ML scale estimation will not be rewarded by the leaderboard number.

Hazard is described by the host as an additive sum of individual hazard contributions: 'Some inspection hazards are major and contribute more to the total score, while some are minor and contribute less. The total score for a property is the sum of the individual hazards.' That is a compound-sum/Tweedie description. It also means the target is integer-valued but not a plain count of equally weighted events.
Far0n's reg:logistic arm divides the target by 69 (div69: y = y / 69.), which implies max(Hazard) = 69 in the training set. Not independently verified against the local table in this run.

Both the 1st-place and 3rd-place pipelines strip the comma before casting: train_test['Field10'].apply(lambda x: x.replace(',', '')).astype(np.int32) in Python, bigD[, Field10 := as.numeric(gsub(",", "", Field10))] in R. PropertyField37 and GeographicField63 carry a SINGLE-SPACE ' ' level that is a missing-value sentinel, not a real category. The 1st-place pipeline maps it explicitly to -1 before label encoding: train_test['PropertyField37'].apply(lambda x: -1 if x == ' ' else x) and the same for GeographicField63. All remaining NaNs are filled with -1 by every published solution (train_test.fillna(-1) / bigD[is.na(bigD)] <- -1). -1 is therefore the universal missing sentinel across the pipelines, and the row-wise count of -1 is itself a feature. For a smooth additive model this is the wrong encoding: -1 sits off the end of the observed range of each column and will drag the spline. Route missingness to an explicit category or a missing-indicator term instead, and rebuild the NaNCount feature from the indicator.

Fold-level AUC noise is large relative to the prize gaps: the 1st-place team saw 'absolute AUC differences up to 0.000085 for a single fold between two submissions with the same CV-mean', and their winning margin over 2nd place on the public LB was 0.00003. 3rd place report meta-level 5-fold std of ~0.00094. data_quirks.description: Every column is scaled and has random noise added by the anonymisation. The 1st place team's central technical finding was that integer-type features can be un-scaled by detecting the per-column scaling factor, and they call this 'a crucial part of our winning solution'. Practical consequence for a smooth model: several float64 columns are latent integer counts on a lattice, so a knot placement chosen from the raw float quantiles will straddle lattice points arbitrarily. Detect the lattice first.

Massive block-structured missingness: 'approximately 40% of data is missing' across 119 of the 131 columns. The missingness itself is informative - competitors added a per-row nan_count feature and treated categorical NA as its own level ('UNKNOWN') rather than imputing. For a GLM/GAM arm this means an explicit missing-indicator or a 'missing' factor level per column, plus the row-level NA count as a numeric term.

Sentinel fills used by successful pipelines: -9999 for all NAs in the CatBoost tutorial (applied before the categorical declaration, so string columns get the literal string too), and -999 for numerics with 'UNKNOWN' for categoricals in tyz910's pipeline. These are conventions the authors chose, NOT sentinels present in the raw file - do not treat -999/-9999 as pre-existing missing codes.

Official data description: 'You are provided with an anonymized dataset containing both categorical and numeric variables available when the claims were received by BNP Paribas Cardif. All string type variables are categorical. There are no ordinal variables.' So every str column in the schema is an unordered factor by declaration, and any integer code must not be treated as ordered either.

v22 has extreme cardinality. The CatBoost tutorial declares a column categorical when nunique() < 30000, a threshold plainly chosen so v22 still qualifies, and it is the only string column singled out by name and excluded from the base pair enumeration so it can anchor the triples instead. No case weights, no exposure, no offset and no date column exist in this dataset. The unit of observation is one claim, the target is a binary approval-route flag, and the metric is unweighted log loss over rows. Do not add a weight or offset term.

Realistic score scale, to calibrate expectations for the additive arm: a fixed CatBoost with zero feature engineering is 0.436 private log loss (rank 31/2920); the best documented public feature set reaches 0.430 (rank 12/2920). A mid-table pipeline (XGBoost plus ExtraTrees blend, ~50 selected features, no interactions) lands at 0.463. So the entire interaction payoff on this dataset is roughly 0.006 of log loss, and the gap between a competent no-interaction model and a competent one is about 0.027.

Pairwise beats higher-order on this dataset specifically: OpenFE report that on BNP 'generating high-order features provides a small improvement in the test score' over first-order only (0.435 -> 0.432 public, 0.432 -> 0.430 private), and conclude 'first-order features are usually more important than high-order ones'. This directly supports a model of smooth mains plus TWO-way tensor interactions, and says third-order terms are worth little.

metric.name: Quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) over 8 ordinal Response levels; w_ij = (i-j)^2/(N-1)^2, kappa = 1 - sum(w*O)/sum(w*E)

target.winners_transform: Two documented routes, both ending in a search over 7 monotone cut-points that maximises QWK. (a) 2nd/4th place: treat Response as a NUMERIC score 1..8 and fit a real-valued regression (plain sklearn LinearRegression for 2nd place; xgboost reg:linear, count:poisson and multi:softmax-expectation for 4th place), then digitise with 7 cutoffs found by fmin_powell / grid search. (b) 1st place: cumulative ordinal decomposition - seven binary models for P(Response > i), i=1..7, and the SUM of the seven probabilities is used as the continuous score, then the same cut-point calibration. 1st place initialises the boundaries from the training Response distribution and does coordinate-wise boundary search until no boundary moves.

proposed_family.reason: The 2nd and 4th place solutions fit Response as a numeric 1 to 8 score with squared error and then search seven cut-points to maximise quadratic weighted kappa; a Gaussian identity-link model on that coding is the like-for-like arm. Poisson with a log link is the documented alternative (private 0.67242 for the 4th place competitor, within 0.001 of his squared-error models), and an ordinal cumulative-link model with seven P(Response > i) fits is the 1st place score construction.

data_quirks.description: DebtRatio was computed by the sponsor as debt / coalesce(MonthlyIncome, 1). On every row where MonthlyIncome is NA the DebtRatio cell therefore holds the RAW MONTHLY DEBT AMOUNT (usually a large integer), not a ratio. This is the single most consequential quirk in the dataset and two top-5 teams exploited it. It also makes DebtRatio bimodal, so one smooth over it mixes two different units.

Corollary measured on the data by a participant: among rows with DebtRatio > 1, an INTEGER DebtRatio implies a missing MonthlyIncome, and those borrowers have a noticeably LOWER bad rate than the non-integer ones. So integer-valued DebtRatio is a usable derived indicator in its own right. The competition admin partially confirmed the mechanism.

Second confirming thread with the observed value pattern: DebtRatio values of exactly 2, 3, ... always have MonthlyIncome = NaN, while the non-integer values in between (2.0004, 2.0006, ..., 2.9946) all have real incomes.

96 and 98 are SENTINEL CODES in the three past-due count columns, not counts. Observed distribution for NumberOfTime30-59DaysPastDueNotWorse: 0:126018, 1:16033, 2:4598, 3:1754, 4:747, 5:342, 98:264, 6:140, 7:54, 8:25, 9:12, 96:5, 10:4, 12:2, 11:1, 13:1 - a clean run to 13 and then a jump to 96/98. The 1st-place team reads them as survey-style 'other / don't know / refused to say' codes. They must be pulled out before any sum, mean or spline over these columns.

RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines is defined as a fraction (balance divided by the sum of credit limits) but ranges to ~50708; the training row quoted on the forum is index 85490 with RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines = 50708. Kaggle's own ruling was to leave it alone ('Yes you just use the data as it is', Jeremy Howard) and the competition admin said it 'can be due to over indebtedness or bad data'. Nathaniel Ramm (1st) offers the mechanism: a closed card with a residual balance and a limit floored at one cent. Practically: log or arctan compress, or split off an 'implausible utilisation' indicator; do not spread spline knots over the empty tail.

The errors-in-data thread carries the concrete offending training row, the observation that DebtRatio > 1 corresponds to MonthlyIncome = NA, and the 1st-place team's closed-account explanation for the utilisation outliers.

age has a long implausible tail: 489 rows with age > 90, 13 rows with age > 100, maximum 109. Participants suggest the ages were computed at an earlier extract date. Cap, or let the penalty handle it, but do not place knots above ~90.

MonthlyIncome contains values that are annual income mistakenly entered in thousands (off by a factor of 1000), per the 5th-place team; and a separate subset are suspiciously round (exact multiples of 1000), which 3rd place flagged as a FEATURE rather than a defect.

Effect sizes are tiny and the public leaderboard was misleading. Private AUC: 1st 0.869558, 2nd 0.869295, 3rd 0.869288, 5th 0.869135, 35th 0.868558 - the whole top 35 spans 0.001 AUC, and the organiser's benchmark at 0.864249 would have ranked ~386 of 970. The public LB used only 30% of the test set; 3rd place was 21st on public and the public leader ('Vsu', 0.86390) finished 9th. A/B a feature with repeated CV over all 150k rows, never with a single hold-out.

Class imbalance was handled by resampling, not by reweighting the likelihood: 3rd place used non-proportional stratified sampling to a balanced set plus randomForest's internal subsampling and gbm observation weights; 1st-place member Eu Jin Lok spent much of the competition trying to make SMOTE work and reports it did NOT work here. Do not assume synthetic minority oversampling helps on this dataset.

Blending convention that mattered: predictions were averaged on the LOGIT scale, not as probabilities and not as ranks ('the average of a bunch of logit predictions works much better than the average rank', 5th place). Relevant only if the known-good arm is blended with anything else.

Replace with NaN and add a DAYS_EMPLOYED_ANOM indicator before any mean, scaling or spline; it is also the only positive value in an otherwise all-negative DAYS_* column.

'XNA' is a missing-value sentinel string, confirmed for CODE_GENDER and ORGANIZATION_TYPE; 365243 is confirmed as a missing-value sentinel for DAYS_EMPLOYED but NOT for SK_ID_CURR. CODE_GENDER == 'XNA' affects only a handful of rows (treat as a rare level or drop those rows); ORGANIZATION_TYPE == 'XNA' is a large block coinciding with the pensioners and is a real level.
Class imbalance: TARGET is 0 on 282,686 rows and 1 on 24,825 rows, an 8.07% positive rate. The winners did not resample; with AUC only the ranking matters.

Marginal correlations with TARGET are all small and the three external scores dominate: EXT_SOURCE_3 -0.179, EXT_SOURCE_2 -0.160, EXT_SOURCE_1 -0.155, DAYS_BIRTH +0.078, DAYS_EMPLOYED +0.075. No single application column is strong, which is why the winners' gains came from interactions and from the joined tables.

OWN_CAR_AGE has an anomalous tail: 3,339 rows report a car age of 60 years or more and default at 8.39% versus 7.21% for the rest. Cap the column or carry an indicator; a spline through that tail will be driven by these rows. OWN_CAR_AGE is also NaN wherever FLAG_OWN_CAR == 'N', so its missingness is structural and perfectly predicted by another column.

Age is conventionally derived as DAYS_BIRTH / -365 (mean about 44 years). All DAYS_* columns are negative day offsets relative to the application date, so their sign is the opposite of the intuitive direction and a monotone constraint set on the raw column points the wrong way.

No exposure, weight or date column exists in application_train.csv - it is described as 'Static data for all applications. One row represents one loan'. So no prior weight and no offset is justified, unlike a typical insurance table.

data_quirks.description: The label is attached to the CARD, not the transaction. Host rule: a reported chargeback marks that card's transaction as isFraud=1, and later transactions linked by user account, email address or billing address are marked fraud too; if nothing is reported within 120 days the transaction counts as legitimate. Measured consequence: of 73,838 training clients with 2+ transactions, 96.9% are all-0, 2.9% all-1 and only 0.2% mixed.

Train/test differ by CLIENT, not by time. Adversarial validation between train and test gives AUC ~1.0, but this is because 68.2% of private-test rows are clients unseen in train (16.4% are seen in both, 15.4% uncertain), not because the fraud process drifts. Validation must therefore test generalisation to unseen clients, e.g. GroupKFold with the client (or the month) as group.

TransactionDT is a timedelta in seconds from a reference, not a timestamp. day = TransactionDT / 86400; the dataset is believed to start on 1 December 2017, and the example client has a card start day of -81 (about 10 September 2017), so D1n can be negative.
D9 is the hour of day, and there is exactly one more D column than C column - both observations come from the 2nd place team's exploration, and D9 is aggregated per client by the 1st place team.

V307 is a rolling one-month cumulative sum of the card's transaction amounts (V307 = V310 + V317 + V320, its counter being V294 + V298 + V285), and many other V columns come in (counter, cumulative-sum) pairs. Such columns are functions of the row's own history, so they are near-duplicates of the client aggregates and must not be treated as independent covariates.

Missingness is structural and heavy (figures from a top-3.5% secondary writeup, not the winners): R_emaildomain ~76% missing, dist2 ~93%, M1-M9 over 50%, addr1/addr2 ~11%, card1 none. The V columns are organised into blocks that share an identical NaN pattern, which is itself the clue to which Vesta feature family they belong to.

train_identity covers only a subset of TransactionIDs, so all id_01..id_38, DeviceType and DeviceInfo columns are missing for the unmatched majority of transactions; the join is a left join on TransactionID.
Amount outlier: at least one training transaction exceeds 30,000 USD; the secondary writeup dropped amounts above 30,000 to avoid fitting the tail. The positive rate is about 3.5%.

No sample weights are provided and none were used; the metric is plain AUC, so nothing needs rebalancing, though the 1st place team notes class weights helped CatBoost while over/under-sampling did not help LGBM or XGB.

Validation designs that the two top teams actually trusted: 1st place used train 4 months / skip 1 / predict 1, train 2 / skip 2 / predict 2, train 1 / skip 4 / predict 1 and 6-fold GroupKFold by month; 2nd place used four expanding-window folds with a deliberate gap (0|2-6, 0-1|3-6, 0-1-2|4-6, 0-1-2-3|5-6) and averaged the AUCs. Any in-fold random CV over-states performance because it lets a client appear in both folds.

metric.name: RMSLE (root mean squared logarithmic error) on price_doc

target.winners_transform: Two distinct transforms are documented. (a) 1st place (Evgeny Patekha): model price per square metre, i.e. fit price_doc / full_sq and multiply the prediction back by full_sq - 'I didn't predict full apartment prices directly, but prices per 1 square meter.' (b) The metric is RMSLE, so the standard competition practice (and the 15th place code) is to work on log1p(price_doc) or on the ratio target with a squared-error objective. The 15th place blend fits BOTH price_doc/full_sq (model_1) and raw price_doc (model_2) and averages them. On top of either, both the 1st place and the 15th place apply a multiplicative level correction to the predictions (the so-called 'magic numbers'), which for the 1st place differ by product_type: 1.05 for Investment and 0.9 for OwnerOccupier.
target.critic_correction: The research report's target claim was marked unsupported. Two corrections apply: the 15th place notebooks use no log transform at all (they fit price_doc/full_sq and raw price_doc under squared error), and Gamma or Tweedie with a log link is not the RMSLE objective, so Gaussian on log1p(price_doc) is the family this catalogue proposes. The metric, the target column and the 1st place price-per-square-metre transform are confirmed.

proposed_family.reason: The metric is RMSLE, and a Gaussian identity-link fit on log1p(price_doc) is that objective exactly. The research report proposed Gamma or Tweedie with a log link first; the critic refuted that ordering because neither is the RMSLE objective, so the catalogue records the Gaussian-on-log arm as the proposal and the Gamma log-link arm as a secondary variant.

data_quirks.description: full_sq contains many outright errors. The 1st place removed it as a direct feature on exactly this ground: 'it contained many mistakes in data'. Expect implausible values at both ends (near-zero and thousands of square metres).
life_sq == full_sq is a sentinel for 'living area not recorded', not a real measurement; the 15th place replaces it with NaN before fitting.

Missing full_sq is imputed with the constant 50 at prediction time, and missing product_type is imputed to Investment, in the 15th place pipeline: 'test1.loc[test1['full_sq'].isnull(),'full_sq'] = 50' and 'test1.loc[test1['product_type'].isnull(),'product_type'] = 1'.

build_year and max_floor carry errors that the 1st place fixed by hand ('I fixed some errors in features with squares, build year and max floor'). A dedicated discussion thread 'What is the meaning of build year 0 or 1?' (topic 32958) confirms sentinel build_year values; only the thread title could be read, not its body.

Roughly 10% of training rows are under-reported (tax-avoidance) prices. Critically, the fake level is NOT a fixed rouble threshold: 'In some areas 2 or 3 million were real prices, in other even 10 million were much lower than market.' Any fixed low-price filter is wrong.

Addresses are approximate for some properties, and several distinct address labels are in reality one place. The 1st place found Basmannoe (kremlin_km==2.90274), Savelki and both Krukovo were one location, and that the Basmannoe geo-coordinates point at a park with no buildings. Correcting these was worth ~0.004 RMSLE.

The host issued corrected train and test files during the competition (the 'Tverskoe issue'). The 15th place repository states its inputs are 'train_sber_corrected.csv - train data after correction from Sberbank' and links discussion 34364. If the local copy is the ORIGINAL train.csv, the Tverskoe rows still carry the error the winners worked from corrected data for.

The test set is chronologically after the training set and sits at a different price level, so an unadjusted model's prediction mean is wrong. Every documented solution applies a multiplicative level correction ('magic numbers'): 1.05/0.9 by product_type for the 1st place, a flat 0.9915 for the 15th place's model_1.

The competition rules explicitly permit look-ahead: 'There are no temporal restrictions: when generating predictions for a particular timestamp, your model may use observations with future-dated timestamps.' External data was also allowed. So a chronological split is a modelling choice here, not a competition constraint - but it is the honest one for a pricing use case.

macro.csv is not present locally. The 1st place tried and failed to model the macro trend from it ('I tried to build model to get trend similar to coefficients that I got from LB probing, and found that we had not enough macro data'), so its absence costs less than the column count suggests - but it does mean the time trend has to be estimated from price_doc itself, exactly as the 1st place did.

The two product_type arms have very different achievable accuracy: the 1st place reports CV ~0.09 for the non-investment arm and ~0.13 for the investment arm, and says his Investment CV was 'amost unusable' with random folds. Use a half-year (8-fold) chronological split, and only after deflating the target to one price level.
